title: Waking, dreaming, sleep, and the fourth
hookLine: Hanuman asks Rama how anyone gets free, and Rama names one short Upanishad about a single night
carry: the self that wakes, dreams and sleeps is brahman
tomorrow: what light do you see by in the dark?

lines: WAKING. DREAMING. SLEEP. AND A FOURTH.
cards: In Ayodhya, after the war, Hanuman sits at Rama's feet and asks what every seeker asks: how does anyone get free? Back in year one you heard Rama's answer: one Upanishad is enough, if you truly take it in.
In the Muktika Upanishad he names that one. The Mandukya. And it isn't about heaven, or battles, or gods.
It's about something you'll do tonight. Lights out, and the to-do list lets go. Pictures start arriving on their own.
Later even the pictures stop. Then morning. Waking, dreaming, deep sleep.

teach.h: AYAM ATMA BRAHMA: THIS SELF IS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: The Mandukya begins with a word from the mantra days just behind us: Om. All this is Om, it says. Then, in its second verse, one of the great sayings of the Upanishads: this Self is Brahman.
Ayam atma brahma. The you behind your eyes is not finally other than the reality behind everything. And this Self, it says, has four quarters.
In paraphrase: the first is waking, knowing outward, enjoying the world of things. The second is dreaming, knowing inward, enjoying what is subtle.
The third is deep sleep, where the sleeper wants nothing and sees no dream. The text doesn't call it empty. It calls it a gathered mass of knowing, full of bliss, the doorway to knowledge.

teach.h: THE FOURTH: NOT IN, NOT OUT. PEACEFUL.
teach.b: And then the fourth, turiya, described mostly by what it is not. Not knowing outward, not knowing inward, not a mass of knowing. Unseen, beyond grasp, peaceful, one without a second.
That, it says, is the Self, and that is what is to be known. Then it maps the four onto Om. The A is waking.
The U is dreaming. The M is deep sleep.

teach.h: A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE.
teach.b: The fourth has no part at all; some teachers hear it as the silence after Om ends.
So every night you pass through three rooms, and the same Self is there in each. Advaita teachers read it this way: freedom isn't a place you travel to. It's knowing what was there all along.
And yoga nidra, resting awake on the borders between those rooms, is one way to notice.

how: Hindus who study Vedanta read the Mandukya Upanishad's four states and its saying 'this Self is Brahman', sometimes with Gaudapada's Karika beside it; some chant Om slowly, resting in the silence after the sound.

o: the deepest dreamless sleep, with no one aware
a mantra chanted to fall asleep faster
the sleep of yoga, aware on the borders of sleep

games.q: the Mandukya's four quarters — tap the pairs.
p: a mass of knowing, the sound M

s: the Mandukya calls deep sleep simply empty

the Mandukya maps the sounds of Om onto states of the Self

games.q: Hanuman asks Rama how anyone gets free. which text does Rama say is enough on its own?
o: a long epic about a war.
the Mandukya, about waking, dream, sleep and the fourth.
games.why: in the Muktika Upanishad, Rama says the Mandukya alone is enough. it follows one Self through every state and says: this Self is Brahman.

practice: Say Om once, slowly, aloud or in the mind: feel the A open in the throat, the U round in the mouth, the M hum at the closed lips.
Then let it end and stay in the quiet after it, letting thoughts come like pictures at the edge of sleep. When it feels right, say Om once more, and rest again in the silence that follows.

wordCard.voice: Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, resting on the borders the Mandukya maps: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth beyond them.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: turiya, the fourth. The Mandukya's name for what lies beyond waking, dream and deep sleep.

carryVoice: Your line: the Self that wakes, dreams and sleeps is Brahman. Tomorrow, a king who keeps asking. Rest well.
